title: Fake Websites
about: Read a web address to see who really owns the page.

cards.situation: Alex messages Sam: "Is this page really Your Bank?"

image.alt: Sam's phone shows a chat with Alex: Email said my card's locked. Tapped the link and this opened. Real?? Under it, a screenshot of a sign-in page with a big Your Bank logo.

cards.prompt: It looks just like Your Bank. **Tap each part** to look closer.

parts.job: Looks just like Your Bank's. But anyone can copy a logo in minutes.
It means what you type is scrambled on the way. Scam sites get padlocks too.
10 minutes! Rushing you, like the scam email.
Asks for secrets. A real bank never asks for your card PIN on a web page.
Look at the end: the name just before the ending (.example) owns the page. Here that's login-check, not Your Bank.

cards.explanation: A copied logo and a padlock prove nothing; the address shows who owns the page.

cards.prompt: Alex types the password into this page. **Who gets it?**

image.alt: The fake page, yourbank.example.login-check.example, with the Your Bank logo and a password typed in; Alex taps Sign in. Below, three choices: Your Bank; login-check; nobody, it's padlocked.
image.revealAlt: The password travels, scrambled on the way, and comes out at login-check's laptop: Got it. Your Bank's building is untouched.

options.text: Nobody: the padlock keeps it safe

cards.explanation: The address says login-check owns the page, and the padlock only scrambles the password on the way.

cards.title: Read the address
cards.body: A fake site can copy a logo, but not the real **web address**. Find the ending (like .example, .com or .com.au) and read the name just before it: that's the owner.

image.alt: The address yourbank.example.login-check.example, taken apart. yourbank.example is a decoy. login-check is the owner: the name just before the ending. .example is the ending. The real address is yourbank.example.

cards.prompt: Alex closes the fake page. **Tap Your Bank's real address.**

image.alt: Your Bank's real address: yourbank.example. Three web addresses, each with a padlock: yourbank.example/signin; login-check.example/signin; yourbank-secure.example/signin.

options.nudge: Find the ending in each, then read the name just before it.
Find the ending in each, then read the name just before it. Is it exactly yourbank?

cards.explanation: The name before the ending is exactly yourbank, so it's Your Bank's.
cards.showAnswer: yourbank.example/signin. The others belong to login-check and yourbank-secure, which isn't the same name.

cards.prompt: This address starts with login: login.yourbank.example. **Tap who owns it.**

image.alt: One big address bar with a padlock: login.yourbank.example. Below, three choices: Your Bank; someone called login; nobody can tell.
image.revealAlt: The address lights up from the right: .example is the ending, yourbank just before it is the owner, and login. in front is just a part of Your Bank's site.

options.nudge: Start from the right: find the ending, then the name just before it.
Start from the right: find the ending, then the name just before it.

cards.explanation: The name just before the ending is yourbank, so it's Your Bank's own page.
cards.showAnswer: Your Bank owns it. Words in front don't change the owner; only the name before the ending counts.

cards.prompt: Your password manager fills in only on real sites. **Here it won't. Why?**

image.alt: Your phone shows a page that looks exactly like Your Bank's sign-in, with its address cut off after the first few letters. The password box is empty, and a key pop-up says: No saved passwords for this site.

options.text: It isn't Your Bank's real address
The manager's broken: type it in
options.nudge: Where does a password manager fill in, and what does it check first?

options.text: Your Bank turned managers off today
options.nudge: Where does a password manager fill in, and what does it check first?

cards.explanation: A password manager reads the whole address for you, so a quiet one is a warning sign.
cards.showAnswer: It isn't Your Bank's real address. Close it and open the Your Bank app or a bookmark instead.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
Logos can be copied and scam sites get padlocks too; only the web address shows who owns a page.

**Try this:** Bookmark the sign-in pages you use, and open them from there.

**Next:** What your posts and photos quietly reveal about you.
